summary: Describes the policies, procedures and history behind cooperation between IEEE 802 and the IETF, such as work on SNMP MIBs and AAA applications. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 7241.

plainLanguage.summary: Two clubs that build different parts of networks agreed on how to work together. This note writes down their rules and how they got friendly. A newer note replaced it.

questions: how do ieee 802 and ietf coordinate
why does eap depend on both organizations
subtitle: How IEEE 802 and IETF coordinate on standards for network hardware and protocols.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802 (which builds local-area network standards) and IETF (which builds Internet standards) have overlapping work, but historically had little coordination, leading to incompatibilities and duplicated effort.
tldr.mechanism: The two organizations established liaison relationships, forums for document review, access to work-in-progress documents, and formal procedures for reviewing each other's work on MIBs, authentication protocols, and other shared technologies.
tldr.outcome: Coordination improved, allowing the organizations to develop higher-quality, more interoperable standards and to avoid conflicts between IEEE 802 and IETF specifications.

today: RFC 4441 was obsoleted by RFC 7241 in June 2014, which updated the relationship procedures as both organizations evolved.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IEEE 802 is a standards organization focused on local and metropolitan area networks (LANs and MANs). The IETF develops protocols for the wider Internet. Since the late 1980s, the two organizations have worked together on technologies that sit at the boundary between network hardware (IEEE 802's domain) and Internet protocols (IETF's domain).

These shared areas include management information bases (MIBs) for network devices, authentication and authorization systems (AAA), and protocols like IEEE 802.1X port-based access control. Without coordination, the two organizations might create incompatible specifications. This document describes the policies and procedures developed to keep them aligned.
sections.plainLanguage: IEEE 802 and the IETF both build network rules. Sometimes their rules overlap. This document explains how they talk to each other so their rules work together.

sections.title: How the Organizations Communicate
sections.content:
The main mechanism is liaison relationships. IETF participants are appointed as liaisons to IEEE 802, and vice versa. These liaisons attend meetings, send formal letters (called liaison statements) between the organizations, and help coordinate work.

Liaison statements are submitted through a formal tool and archived so both organizations can track them. When IEEE 802 sends a liaison letter to IETF, it is recorded, responded to, and made public. Similarly, IETF requests sent to IEEE 802 are handled through official channels. The two organizations also maintain a shared mailing list to announce new work proposals so each can review the other's upcoming projects early.
sections.plainLanguage: IEEE 802 assigns people to watch IETF work, and IETF assigns people to watch IEEE 802. They send official letters to each other when something important happens.

sections.title: Document Access and Review
sections.content:
IEEE 802 publishes finished standards for free (older than six months). However, work-in-progress documents are restricted. To help IETF groups collaborate, IEEE 802 allows its working group chairs to grant IETF members access to draft documents. An IETF working group chair can request a username and password to access IEEE 802 work-in-progress, then share it with participants in the working group.

In return, IETF participants are welcome to comment on IEEE 802 ballot processes. The two organizations also review each other's technical documents: IETF review EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) and AAA standards developed by IEEE 802, and IEEE 802 reviews IETF documents on wireless access point control and other topics.
sections.plainLanguage: The two groups show each other their work before it is finished. IETF people can read IEEE 802 drafts if they ask. IEEE 802 people read IETF standards and give feedback.

sections.title: Shared Technology Areas: MIBs and Authentication
sections.content:
A key collaboration area is Management Information Bases (MIBs). MIBs are the data models used by SNMP, the Internet's main management protocol. IEEE 802 devices need to be managed via SNMP, but SNMP is an IETF technology. Rather than have IEEE 802 develop MIBs independently, the organizations agreed that IEEE 802 would develop MIBs following IETF guidelines, and IETF's MIB quality reviewers (MIB Doctors) would provide feedback.

Another key area is authentication and authorization. IEEE 802.1X defines port-based network access control, and IEEE 802.11 uses the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) for wireless security. Both depend on IETF's RADIUS protocol and EAP standard. The two organizations coordinate through liaison arrangements and joint reviews to ensure these technologies work together.
sections.plainLanguage: IEEE 802 builds network devices that need management. They use IETF's SNMP language to describe them. IETF experts check the descriptions are correct. For security, IEEE 802 uses IETF's authentication rules.

sections.title: Relationship History
sections.content:
The relationship began in the late 1980s with the Bridge MIB for IEEE 802.1D (spanning tree). The IETF Bridge working group developed the MIB because the IEEE specification lacked the implementation detail needed. Over the decades, MIB development grew to cover Ethernet interfaces, hubs, media attachment units, and other devices.

Cooperation became more formal when IEEE 802.11 began work on wireless security. In 2002, the IETF created the EAP working group to develop and clarify the Extensible Authentication Protocol that IEEE 802 needed. Through liaison arrangements, IETF EAP work and IEEE 802.1X development proceeded in parallel, with each informing the other.
sections.plainLanguage: The two groups learned to work together over many years. They found that talking early and reading each other's work made better standards.

sections.title: Benefits and Lessons
sections.content:
Coordination between IEEE 802 and IETF has produced higher-quality, more interoperable standards. When problems were found in early specifications (such as security issues in IEEE 802.1X state machines), the liaison relationship allowed the groups to work together to clarify and fix them.

Key lessons include: (1) starting coordination early, before work is finalized, is better than trying to fix incompatibilities later; (2) allowing members to participate in both organizations helps; (3) shared technical reviews catch errors and improve clarity; and (4) formal liaison arrangements with archived communications ensure problems do not fall through the cracks.
sections.plainLanguage: When IEEE 802 and IETF talk to each other early and review each other's work, both groups make better standards. They found out that having a few people in both groups is really helpful.
